<p class="mw-kicker">Marketing in 3 · Issue 40 · Week of 12 October 2026</p>
<figure class="mw-hero"><picture><source type="image/webp" sizes="(max-width: 900px) 100vw, 900px" srcset="../../images/web/issue-40-trend-atypicality-960.webp 960w, ../../images/web/issue-40-trend-atypicality-1600.webp 1600w"><img src="../../images/issue-40-trend-atypicality.jpg" alt="A smartphone on a tripod in a dark studio, its screen showing a camera app ready to record, with a blurred red and white shape in the foreground" width="1600" height="900" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async"></picture><figcaption>Same trend, same camera. What matters is what you do differently in front of it. Photo: Roman Manshin on Unsplash.</figcaption></figure>
<section class="mw-answer" aria-label="Short answer"><h2>The short answer</h2><p>Put your own spin on it. Across 85,000 TikTok dance-trend videos, those that differed more from the rest of the trend earned more likes per view, even for the same creator. Experiments confirmed that the difference was the cause, and a test with 38 real creators agreed. The edge appears once viewers have seen the trend enough to spot the twist, and it came from deviations later in the video.</p></section>
<section class="mw-takeaways"><h2>Key takeaways</h2><ul><li>More atypical videos earned more likes per view. Among the videos in the study, the most atypical earned about 112 likes per 1,000 views, against about 92 for the most typical.</li><li>The advantage grew as a trend got older and more videos were out there. In an experiment, the twist only paid off when viewers had seen the trend first.</li><li>Twists in the last part of a video went with more engagement, and twists in the first seconds did not.</li><li>Viewers did not get bored of the standard version. They saw the twisted one as more unique and its creator as more creative.</li></ul></section>
<section id="what-the-researchers-did"><h2>What the researchers did</h2><p>Following a trend is one of the most common ways brands and creators try to get seen on short-video platforms. The question
is how to do it. Copy the dance move for move and ride the wave, or add your own twist? Content creators asked by the
authors were split. About half said to stay close to the trend, and about a quarter said to deviate.</p><p>The team, from Swiss universities and Wharton, needed a way to measure how different one video is from others in a trend. They
built a video-analysis tool, MUVID, that turns each video, with its sound and movement, into a set of numbers. A video&#x27;s atypicality is then
how far those numbers sit from earlier videos in the same trend.</p><p>They applied it to more than 85,000 TikTok dance videos grouped into around 1,500 trends, then ran three experiments, one of
them a field test with real creators, to check whether the pattern was cause and not coincidence.</p>
<dl class="mw-facts"><div><dt>Data</dt><dd>86,244 TikTok dance videos in 1,548 trends, uploaded between 2015 and 2022</dd></div><div><dt>Measure</dt><dd>Distance of each video from earlier videos in its own trend, and likes divided by views</dd></div><div><dt>Controls</dt><dd>Creator, trend and month effects, plus video quality, dance quality and creator size</dd></div><div><dt>Experiments</dt><dd>Two online studies with 201 and 494 adults, and a field test with 38 TikTok creators</dd></div><div><dt>Tool</dt><dd>MUVID is open source and has a web app for measuring video similarity</dd></div></dl>
</section>
<section id="more-different-more-liked"><h2>More different, more liked</h2><p>In the large dataset, the more a video differed from its trend, the more likes it earned per view. Videos more than one standard
deviation more atypical than average earned about 112 likes per 1,000 views. Average ones earned about 101, and the most
typical earned about 92.</p><p>The link held when the authors compared a creator with themselves, which rules out simply being a talented or popular creator.
It also held after allowing for video and dance quality, and across other checks such as matching typical and atypical videos on
their traits.</p><p>The effect per video is small. One standard deviation of extra atypicality went with about 2.5% higher odds that a viewer liked
the video. The authors point out that on a platform with huge volume it adds up. For a creator with 15,000 views per
video, shifting from a typical to an atypical video meant roughly 69 extra likes.</p>

Least and most atypical are more than 1 SD below and above the average within a trend.</p></figure>

<section id="the-twist-needs-an-audience-that-knows-the-trend"><h2>The twist needs an audience that knows the trend</h2><p>You can only see a difference if you know what the normal version looks like. The authors predicted that atypicality would pay
off more when viewers had seen lots of videos from the trend. In the data it did. The more videos a trend had already collected,
the stronger the link with engagement.</p><p>An experiment tested this directly. Participants saw five videos from a trend, or five unrelated videos, and then a focal video that either
copied the dance or used a different one. After the trend videos, 34% chose to engage with the atypical version against 18% for the
typical one. With no trend exposure, the two were level at about 17%.</p><p>A follow-up asked why. Viewers did not tire of the standard version. They simply judged the twisted version as more unique, and
its creator as more creative.</p>

</section>
<section id="where-in-the-video-to-deviate"><h2>Where in the video to deviate</h2><p>The authors split each video into its first and last five seconds. Atypicality in the last part was linked to more
engagement. Atypicality in the opening seconds was not.</p><p>Their reading is that viewers first need to recognise the trend, and a surprise only lands after the pattern has been
established. The authors describe this as suggestive and worth a dedicated experiment.</p>
</section>
<section id="a-field-test-with-real-creators"><h2>A field test with real creators</h2><p>In the first experiment, 201 online participants watched five faithful trend videos and one focal video. Among those who saw an atypical
version of the focal video, 24% chose to engage, against about 13% for the typical version.</p><p>The final test went to the platform itself. Thirty-eight creators each made two videos for two trends, one in the typical
style and one with a twist, posting them about three days apart. With creator effects held constant, the atypical videos had about 10%
higher odds of a like per view. This was the weakest result in the paper, and it came from small videos, averaging 783 views.</p>
</section>
<section id="how-to-apply-it" class="mw-howto"><p class="mw-rsg-kicker">Marketing in 3 steps</p><h2>Ready. Set. Market.</h2><div class="mw-rsg"><div class="mw-phase"><div class="mw-phase-dot" aria-hidden="true">1</div><div class="mw-phase-tag"><span class="mw-phase-name">Ready</span><span class="mw-phase-sub">Decide and prepare</span></div><ul class="mw-rsg-steps"><li><strong>Pick a trend your audience already knows.</strong> Choose one that has been around for at least a few weeks and that your own followers have already seen. Check by scrolling its page and counting how many videos from different accounts use it.</li><li><strong>Map the standard version.</strong> Watch twenty videos of the trend and write down the elements nearly all of them share, such as setting, moves, outfit, camera angle and ending.</li></ul></div><div class="mw-phase"><div class="mw-phase-dot" aria-hidden="true">2</div><div class="mw-phase-tag"><span class="mw-phase-name">Set</span><span class="mw-phase-sub">Build it</span></div><ul class="mw-rsg-steps"><li><strong>Choose one twist.</strong> Change one element, no more. Keep the part that makes the trend recognisable, and make the change something a viewer can spot in a second.</li><li><strong>Save the twist for the end.</strong> Open the video the way everyone else does, then break away in the final few seconds. Film one version with the twist at the start and one with it at the end.</li></ul></div><div class="mw-phase"><div class="mw-phase-dot" aria-hidden="true">3</div><div class="mw-phase-tag"><span class="mw-phase-name">Market</span><span class="mw-phase-sub">Launch and measure</span></div><ul class="mw-rsg-steps"><li><strong>Make a faithful version too.</strong> Film a straight copy with the same person, location, lighting and caption. Post the copy and the twist about three days apart, and swap which goes first the next time.</li><li><strong>Compare likes per view.</strong> After a week, divide likes by views for each video. Repeat with three different trends before you change your approach, and keep the twist if it wins at least two of the three.</li></ul></div></div></section>
<section id="what-to-expect"><h2>What to expect</h2><ul class="mw-list"><li><strong>A modest gain per video.</strong> The average lift is small, so look for it over many posts and not in a single result.</li><li><strong>A bigger edge on mature trends.</strong> The longer a trend runs, the more a copy blends in.</li><li><strong>Recognisable twists only.</strong> A change that viewers cannot spot as a difference gives no advantage.</li><li><strong>Quality still matters.</strong> The twist helped when dance and video quality were held equal, and it will not rescue a poor video.</li></ul></section>
<section id="where-it-does-not-work"><h2>Where it does not work</h2><ul class="mw-list"><li><strong>One kind of trend.</strong> All the videos were dance trends on TikTok. Other formats, such as transformations or brand challenges, were not tested.</li><li><strong>Likes are not sales.</strong> The outcome is likes per view, with no data on follows, clicks or purchases.</li><li><strong>Small field test.</strong> The creator experiment had 38 creators and modest views, and its result was borderline.</li><li><strong>Data from 2015 to 2022.</strong> Platform algorithms and audience habits may have moved on since.</li></ul></section>
<section id="questions"><h2>Questions marketers ask</h2><div class="mw-faq"><h3>Should brands copy TikTok trends exactly?</h3><p>Not in this evidence. Videos that put their own spin on a trend earned more likes per view than close copies, and experiments suggest the twist caused the difference (Bravin, Clegg, Hofstetter, Pouly &amp; Berger, 2026, Journal of Marketing).</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>How different does a trend video need to be?</h3><p>The paper found the benefit even for moderate deviations. The twist needs to be noticeable to viewers who know the trend, and the authors did not test how far is too far.</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>When in a video should the twist come?</h3><p>Later. Deviations in the final seconds were linked to more engagement and deviations in the opening seconds were not, though the authors call this suggestive.</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>Does this work for a new trend?</h3><p>Less well. The advantage grew with the number of videos in a trend, and in an experiment it disappeared when viewers had not seen the trend first.</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>What is MUVID?</h3><p>An open-source video analysis tool the authors built. It turns videos into numbers that capture picture, movement and sound, so you can measure how similar two videos are. A web app lets you upload videos and see how typical each one is.</p></div></section>
<section id="also-new"><h2>Also new this week</h2><div class="mw-also"><article><p class="mw-also-src"><em>International Journal of Research in Marketing</em> · 2026</p><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijresmar.2025.07.005">Breaking the mold: how visual atypicality shapes brand-generated image virality</a></h3><p class="mw-also-au">Adam &amp; Yang</p><p>Using machine learning on 60,669 apparel images and 4,087 car images, plus an experiment, this study finds that visually atypical brand images spread further for low-heritage brands because they entertain, and spread less for high-heritage brands because they clash with expectations. Check your brand&#x27;s age before you break the mould.</p></article><article><p class="mw-also-src"><em>Journal of Advertising Research</em> · 2026</p><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/00218499.2026.2670019">How to Make Advertising on Social Media Memorable: Stand Out or Get Lost</a></h3><p class="mw-also-au">Walter, Stocchi, Ward, &amp; Romaniuk</p><p>Two online experiments on in-feed ads find that image-based creative earns higher ad recall than text-based creative, and that text-based creative lowers correct brand recall. Pairing creative type against the type of brand element, for example text creative with a visual brand asset, recovers some of the loss, especially among non-buyers and for larger brands. Lead with an image.</p></article></div></section>

Atypicality and Engagement on Social Media. <em>Journal of Marketing</em>, <em>90</em>(5), 187-204. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/00222429261466668">https://doi.org/10.1177/00222429261466668</a></p><p class="mw-note">This brief is written for practitioners from the published article.
